| [LIT-035](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-035.md) v2 | The ergodicity solution of the cooperation puzzle | Peters et al. If N entities' resources follow GBM (drift μ, volatility σ, independent noise), then pooling and sharing equally every step leaves the drift at μ, cuts the volatility to σ/√N (Eq. 3.9), and raises each member's time-average growth rate from μ − σ²/2 to μ − σ²/(2N) (Eq. 4.1). The premium is (σ²/2)(1 − 1/N) (Eq. 4.2). With pairwise correlation ρ the effective volatility is σ√((1 + (N−1)ρ)/N), and the large-N limit is μ − σ²ρ/2 (Eqs. 5.12–5.13). | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-059](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-059.md)); worth reading as the clearest short derivation of the risk-pooling (geometric-mean) advantage of sharing under multiplicative noise. The mathematics is correct and self-contained. The framing claim, that this "solves" the cooperation puzzle and makes cooperation the default, rests on the model's zero-cost, no-cheating assumptions, and the paper's own citations (McCloskey, Winterhalder, Uitdehaag, Kennedy et al.) show the core result was already known. |
| [LIT-047](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-047.md) v2 | Is It Good to Cooperate? Testing the Theory of Morality-as-Cooperation in 60 Societies | Curry et al. (2019), DOI-10.1086/701478. In the ethnographic records of the 60-society HRAF Probability Sample, seven cooperative behaviours predicted by game theory are morally valenced positively in 961 of 962 observations (99.9%). Coding 3,460 eHRAF paragraphs on the 60 Probability Sample Files societies found 962 morally valenced mentions of seven cooperative behaviours, 961 of them positive. The one negative is Chuuk admiration of open theft as dominance. Presence varied widely by domain: property 54/60 (90%), kin 47 (78%), group 44 (73%), reciprocity 43 (72%), respect 35 (58%), bravery 32 (53%), fairness 9 (15%). | [LIT-067](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-067.md) v2 | A Social Equilibrium Existence Theorem | Debreu (1952), DOI-10.1073/pnas.38.10.886. Debreu proves existence of an equilibrium for an "abstract economy" (generalized game), in which each agent's feasible set A_ι(ā_ι) depends on the others' actions. The conditions: each action set 𝔄_ι is a contractible polyhedron; A_ι has a closed graph with non-empty compact values; f_ι is continuous on the graph into the extended reals; the value function φ_ι(ā_ι) = max f_ι is continuous; and each best-response set M_ā_ι is contractible. The proof applies the Eilenberg–Montgomery/Begle fixed-point theorem to the product best-response map. A Remark replaces the joint continuity of φ_ι with continuity (lower hemicontinuity) of A_ι plus a compact graph. A Corollary gives a saddle-point theorem that contains Kakutani's and von Neumann's. | Active — read in full 2026-09-25 ([NOTE-037](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-037.md)); the original existence theorem for generalized (constrained) games, underlying Arrow–Debreu (1954). Short, fully self-contained, and still the canonical citation. Later results (Shafer–Sonnenschein 1975; the generalized-Nash literature) weaken its hypotheses but do not supersede it as the source. |
